Razer Reclusa X Mini 65% gaming keyboard review
summary: A budget mini keeb that somehow manages to feel high-end.
body: While Razer makes some excellent headsets, laptops, and gaming mice, I've never been particularly keen on its keyboards. They tend to be decent devices overall, but are usually expensive enough that you can get more bang for your buck from the competition. However, there's a new budget offering in town from the big green snake, and it's called the Razer Reclusa X Mini 65%. Those of you familiar with keyboard percentage figures (and the term "mini") will likely deduce that this is a small keeb. There's no numpad to be found here, but at least you get all the main keys needed for day to day usage. It doesn't feel constrictive to type on, and it sure is a good-looking device—but the main thing that impresses me is the build quality, especially given the MSRP. This is a $50 / £60 gaming keyboard, but it feels more expensive than that. The doubleshot ABS keycaps are crisp, the switches are meaty, and its diminutive frame resists flexing to an admirable degree. If you told me this sharp little keyboard retailed for $80, I would absolutely believe you. For $50 at full price? I think it's a damn good bit of gaming hardware for the cash. The specs sheet isn't particularly impressive, I'll …

title: I applied DLSS 5 to my Miku Hatsune game of choice, and I have some regrets
summary: Welcome to anime Hell.
body: For the time being, DLSS5 is only officially available via Nvidia's 50-series cards. The company has said in the past the neural rendering tech will eventually come to 40-series cards too , but I simply couldn't wait. Having now witnessed multiple passes of the upscaling tech applied to my anime-style game of choice, I have some regrets. To be clear, the only way to get DLSS5 working with my Nvidia RTX 4070 Super is through completely unofficial means. You can scour the internet for the files you need, though there are some software options that automate the process. For this unholy experiment, I used DLSS5 Manager and went to town with its adjustable 'Live Flow' function. My game of choice for this unsanctioned exercise is Hatsune Miku: Project Diva Mega Mix+. This game has an anime-adjacent art style that DLSS 5 has no business upscaling, but I'm not letting that stop me. Before finagling a way to apply DLSS5 to this game, it ran at a fairly solid 60 fps (though that's a best case scenario largely dependent on which song you're playing—if you're a Project Diva sicko, you know what I mean). With Live Flow active, my frame rate tanked to the point that pressing timed button prompt…

title: Bethesda says that Obsidian's 'creative identity' will be preserved, just months after multiple projects were cancelled and it was told to make a Fallout game
summary: I don't know about that one, chief.
body: Listen, you can say what you want about Avowed—I wouldn't even blame you if you didn't like it, or much of what has come out of Obsidian's recent catalogue. There's even a tiny, selfish scrap of my gamer heart that's secretly very glad that Obsidian is working on a new Fallout game, again . But this is pretty rich, given the grinder that Obsidian's been put through in the past few months. As a reminder, in July, 25% of Obsidian's staff was laid off during Xbox's ongoing, brutal "reset", totalling around 52 employees. When this happened, a sequel to Avowed was cancelled, along with multiple unannounced games. More recently, Obsidian's being folded into Bethesda . Now, in fairness to Braff, it's entirely possible that this particular merging did not ruin Obsidian's ability to express itself. It's entirely possible that the post-bloodletting Obsidian we were left with in July and the one currently under Bethesda now are pretty much interchangeable. However, the idea that Obsidian's creative identity has been respected by these moves overall is laughable—cancelling multiple projects is the opposite of that, actually. Making it work on a franchise it hasn't really touched in 16 years i…

title: Alienware is working on a fix for the one thing that stops its new 39-inch 5K2K OLED gaming monitor from being perfect
summary: This fix could hurt my wallet.
body: The Alienware AW3926QW is undoubtedly my favourite monitor of the moment , maybe even ever. It has just one problem that prevented me from giving it an unambiguous buy recommendation. And now it seems Alienware is about to fix it. The AW3926QW is of course a 39-inch 5K2K OLED masterpiece. It's huge, it has the pixel density of a 32-inch 4K panel and it comes with LG's very latest Tandem WOLED panel tech complete with RGB-stripe subpixels for purists like me. It's even relatively affordable (given its specs) at around $1,100 . There was just one problem. As I explained in my review, "during gaming the edges of the panel gradually dim ever so slightly," an issue generally referred to as "vignetting." The reason why this happens comes down to a feature called CPC, or Convex Power Control. "It’s an LG Display WOLED panel protection feature and dims all four edges of the display to help prevent burn-in. As far as I am aware, it can't be toggled on or off on this Alienware, but if CPC is causing the vignette issue, it should be easy to address in a firmware update. Broadly, I don't think this is a hardware limitation, but a configuration issue," I explained. Turns out that was correct, …

title: Microsoft's approach to age verification in Australia is further proof that Valve is taking the everloving piss
summary: Valve, are you hearing this?
body: Many are justifiably annoyed about Steam's new age verification requirements in Australia. Whereas most platforms and shopfronts offer several ways to verify one's age, Valve offers only one, and it's amusingly ill-suited to the Australian market. To prove that you're over 18 years old and thus, legally allowed to purchase games like Metal Gear Solid 4, Doom Eternal or Rimworld, you need to provide details for an active credit card. The problem? Very few Australians use credit cards. Even if you opened your Steam account as far back as 2003 and own a handful of R18+ games already, Steam will still require that credit card. I don't want to big up Microsoft for doing slightly more than the bare minimum, but an email I received overnight does at least cast renewed light on how terrible Valve's approach is. An email from Microsoft regarding my "Microsoft Age Verification Status" had this to say: "Due to your longstanding account activity, we’ve estimated your profile to be an adult account and updated its age verification status to “Verified.” At this time, you are no longer required to complete further age verification for uninterrupted access to features across certain Microsoft pro…

title: My first MMO character #2: Joshua Wolens
summary: My first MMO character #2: Joshua Wolens
body: My first MMO character was... Karokan, Half-elf Something Born: 1999 Game: EverQuest Karokan's is a simple tale. When I was six years old, I saw my dad having a good time in a then-new release called EverQuest. Obviously, I wanted in on that, and badgered pops into helping me make a character. My dad played a gnome magician, but I was revulsed by the idea of being as short in the game as I then was in real life. Also, magicianry sounded complicated. I settled on a half-elf whose class I no longer remember, and came up with a basically random series of syllables to serve as a name. And then! I went nowhere. I was terrified . I wasn't so much scared of dying (though I was a bit scared of dying) but of getting lost. EverQuest felt impossibly vast, and I knew for sure that the second I stepped out of Freeport I'd never be able to find my way back. So I spent Karokan's life just outside the city gates, fighting orcs and rats, and never venturing further. It was a simple life, but a happy one. (Read the full article here)

title: I apologize in advance for this, but: Introducing Drillposting
summary: This is all my mind is capable of right now.
body: The study of philosophy is powerful because you can map its insights onto any aspect of life today, just as you could a hundred or a thousand years ago. French philosopher Descartes, for example, pioneered the theory of mind-body dualism, writing "I have a clear and distinct idea of myself, in so far as I am simply a thinking, non-extended thing... and on the other hand I have a distinct idea of body... accordingly, it is certain that I am really distinct from my body, and can exist without it." Descartes was born about 300 years too early to experience jetlag, but he was definitely onto something. After flying home from Japan, where I spent a few days shooting for the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct , I found my separated body and mind capable of little in the way of cogent thought. title: Shoot the tires, please
summary: Wardogs Humvees are a menace with a glaring weakness.
body: Humvees are a nasty threat in Wardogs. They're fast, have thick enough armor to withstand multiple RPGs, and usually come with a machinegun nest that can easily mow down a squad of infantry in a single reload. But they have a pretty huge weakness that, two weeks in, many players in my matches are unaware of: Shoot the tires. Like, with anything. Popping just one tire will cut the Humvees max speed by over half, and popping two will slow it to a crawl. This won't destroy the vehicle or even interrupt the gunner, but it will make it easier to get an unarmored angle on the gun nest and force the driver to make a tough choice: limp out of danger or go for a very risky repair. As YouTuber Min Max Lab helpfully tested , it takes just eight 5.56 bullets (the ammo used by Wardogs' free starter rifle) to pop a tire , so even a single soldier can deal enough damage to ruin a driver's day. I haven't managed to ruin two tires by myself, but popping one is often enough to convince the Humvee to disengage for repairs. Be sure to watch that whole video below for more useful data, like which guns are best for tire destruction (shotguns are quite good), which direction you should shoot from to inc…

title: Sometimes it's fun to hit a scorpion with a club for 38 seconds

body: Like many others who carry the spiritual stain of prior MMO contact, I've been spending some time in the WoW: Forever beta. After piloting a freshly-minted orc through the introductory quests in the Valley of Trials, I emerged into the wider Durotar scrubland where I soon entered into combat with a hostile scorpion that had strayed too close to the road I was following to Razor Hill. For the next 38 consecutive seconds, I did nothing but watch my orc slowly bludgeon that scorpion to death with a wooden club. And reader, I say this with full sincerity: Those were 38 seconds of peak gaming. (Image credit: Blizzard) I haven't just been playing Forever to sample Blizzard's distillation of year one WoW nostalgia. I've been testing a conviction that I recently forwarded after a week with Star Wars Galaxies: a belief that MMOs would be better off if they rediscovered their lost willingness to burn more of our time. (Image credit: Blizzard) My half-minute and change of scorpid combat has left me feeling pretty confident in the hypothesis. summary: My first MMO character #1: Harvey Randall
body: My first character was... Leetman, Human Rogue Born: ~2004-2006 Game: World of Warcraft My first ever character was in World of Warcraft, after—as my bio states—I pretty much begged my parents to give me a WoW subscription, and was rewarded for my articulation with a proper WoW account and a life-changingly debilitating enthusiasm for videogames. And while I did technically have a Runescape character before this, I can't remember 'em, so Leetman is here. I was not a good rogue. In my defense, I was 10 years old—but I didn't level my poisons, I didn't reach level cap, and the height of my career was spent futzing around Un'Goro Crater. I did, however, manage to get the gold for a mount, which made me feel pretty swanky. That was a big deal back in the day. Leetman would eventually be traded out for the troll shaman Earthborn when The Burning Crusade rolled around, but I shall remember him fondly. title: I don't care what you lot say, the side buttons on a mouse are for copy and paste (on desktop)
summary: There are dozens of us! Dozens!
body: The PC Gamer hardware team got into a disagreement last week. We were sat around in the office chatting about Razer's new MMO gaming mouse and how we wouldn't know what to do with all its buttons (it has 12). That got us onto the topic of what we do with the two side buttons more commonly found across gaming mice. Turns out, the team I've worked with for years, who I thought I could trust, who I've shared a laugh with, who I thought were my friends, are complete and utter fools. As are most of you—soz. They reckon the best use of the two side buttons are forwards and back, ie. for browsing the web. That tends to be the default assignment for gaming mice out of the box, which goes to show the lack of ingenuity on their part. We asked you lot what you thought about this very important question in the form of a poll. It read: "Jacob wants to know if there are people like him, so do you have your mouse side button set to forward/back or copy/paste?" The results are pretty surprising. Not for the overwhelming majority of you that use these buttons for forward and back (1,343), but the near two hundred kindred spirits—fellow travellers—that are with me on the whole copy and paste thing.…

title: I crammed 20 anime figures inside my gaming PC to see how it affects thermal performance. Yes, you can call me a scientist now
summary: Asking the important questions.
body: During all my time at PC Gamer, there has been but one idea that feels a bit like flying too close to the sun. I am, of course, talking about cramming as many anime figurines as I can into my PC and monitoring the impact on performance. Thankfully, I've got the figurines, a Hyte Y40 PC case with tool-free, pop-off panels, and an otherwise engaged editor. My methodology is straightforward enough: I'm going to gradually add figurines to the inside of my gaming PC, running FurMark 2 to track any thermal fluctuations. Each time I add more figures, I'll run both the 1080p and the 1440p benchmark presets. First, let's establish the base line: I'm testing on the iBuyPower RDY Y40 Valorant VCTA R003 . On the temperate September day I carried out testing, my RTX 4070 Super enjoyed an ambient temperature of about 34°C / 93.2°F. Without even a whiff of anime inside the PC case, temps shot up to 83°C / 181.4°F under a 100% GPU load in Furmark 2. And, let me tell ya, our Jacob really wasn't kidding when he said those iBuyPower fans get loud under load. The 1080p benchmark returned a score of 11568, and 195 fps. title: AMD starts the ball rolling for GDDR7 in next-gen GPUs with small code adjustment in its Linux drivers
summary: My money is still on RDNA 5 launching by the end of next year.
body: AMD has filed its latest driver patches for Linux and included within those are the first indication of support for GDDR7. As spotted by Phoronix , the AMDGPU patch specifically adds the identifier "GDDR7" to the driver. It's only a small change—a single line in a pile of code for the company's open source GPU driver—yet it aligns with our expectations of new GPUs. The existing 9000 series uses GDDR6, while Nvidia has already moved on to GDDR7 with the RTX 50-series. Even with the ongoing memory crisis, it seems likely that AMD will also move to GDDR7 with the next generation. These patch notes support that view. AMD also added further support for an as-yet unreleased architecture, such as Display Core Next 6 back in July. We're expecting RDNA 5 around the end of 2027 (I still have hope) or pushing into 2028. Current rumours reckon we'll see just a couple of cards in a year's time, with a wider line-up to follow along afterwards. This aligns with the expected launch of next-gen consoles, built on a semi-custom version of that same Radeon architecture. summary: I'm simply built different.
body: I wouldn't take the overtime. The fact that Bryan was forced down this spiral of blood, guts, and tears just because he thought he could make a bit more cash is simultaneously the most realistic and tragic aspect of the new Resident Evil movie. And honestly, I get it. Who doesn't need a bit of extra money right now? So if my hands were really tied and I didn't have any choice about taking the package into Raccoon City, here's what I'd really do differently. Spoilers ahead for the Resident Evil film (Image credit: Sony Pictures) Don't call and drive. Even if your girlfriend's angry at you, jeopardising your safety on an icy road is never the answer. I wouldn't have thrown the ladder at the dog because that's not nice. Although I also wouldn't get that close to it. Getting a snack is a good shout although I'd miss out the milk as I'm lactose intolerant. No way in hell I'd open the door in the RV. I'd have snatched those car keys so fast. In the interest of preserving bullets, I'd have taken a close range shot at the padlock first . Take the stairs, man. Yes, I would have complained about it the whole way up, but the elevator is out of order for a reason. I would like to think that I…

title: Valve shadow dropped chicken pets into CS2
summary: The egg came first.
body: You'd think the most exciting thing to happen in Counter-Strike 2 today would be its new Rush Hour update , complete with a new "fast-paced" mode, or perhaps the fact that you can now silent reload. But you would be wrong, because Rush Hour has been overshadowed by pet chickens. Chickens aren't new to CS2, they've been clucking around some maps for ages now, you could even walk up to them and get them to follow you. But this is different. You can now get an egg in your weekly drop that's untradeable and will consume both of your allotted drops for the week. After a week of the egg sitting in your inventory it should hatch into a chick. But I know what you're thinking: "All you get is a pet chick that you can inspect? That doesn't sound very CS2" you would be right, except for the fact that if you look after your chick and feed it chicken feed it can grow up into a chicken with various skins with different levels of rarity; now that's CS2. There's a normal brown chicken, a white non-bearded silkie, and a tan polish chicken. But it doesn't stop there because there's also apparently 35 various rarities of these chickens which come in different skins. There's bright blue, purple-yello…

title: I have fallen to my own hubris
summary: I thought it would be so simple.
body: I have made the choice to min-max in WoW: Forever , something which I am starting to regret, because oh no, my hubris. See, Blizzard will be raising the level cap sometime soon to 30, and I decided I'd complete a bunch of quests, but not turn them in. But I'd forgotten that a lot of Vanilla-era quests involve picking up quest items. And I only have eight-slot bags. Help me. (Image credit: Blizzard)
